legacy_conversion_note: Original source (source/Y1/Session 7/Driving Age/Case Study_ Driving Age.docx + Guide Notes.docx) is a real bill-format case: the fictional Congresswoman Olivia Edmunds, her rural/urban district, HB 3320's real bill-text excerpt (the source docx reproduces an actual Arizona legislative bill format), the requirement to build a scatterplot with a line of best fit and its algebraic equation, and the Challenge boilerplate structure are all preserved from the source. Per cases/_concepts/LEGACY_DILEMMA_LOCKS_2026-08-20.md (HIGH confidence lock), the original three-option dilemma (AYE at 18 / AYE with an unspecified amended age / NAY at 15.5) is narrowed to the locked binary: AYE at 18 vs. NAY at 15.5 -- the vague 'amendment to some other age' option is dropped, it was never a concrete choice. The original case gave students an open scatterplot assignment with no supplied dataset and no defined primary metric; this conversion supplies a real, sourced dataset (Appendix B: IIHS 2024 driver-age-vs-fatality-rate table) for the mandatory scatterplot/line-of-best-fit/linear-equation deliverables, and constructs a new primary metric (net two-year family dollar cost) because the original case's implicit comparison -- delayed licensure being 'safer' -- does not survive contact with its own best real data: the IIHS table actually shows the fatal-crash rate per 100,000 population *rising*, not falling, from age 16 through 19, which undercuts rather than supports a simple 'raising the age reduces risk' framing (this rise reflects rising driving exposure with age, not rising per-mile risk, and is disclosed as such in Appendix B and used as the case's Twist -- see FACILITATOR.md). Per SPEC.md section 2, the case is built around a metric with a real, close, current, and honestly derived margin (net family dollar cost: added chauffeuring cost under Option A vs. added insurance cost under Option B) rather than forcing the original's unworkable safety-only framing. The constituent poll (240 respondents, 70%/20%/35%/32% splits) is the source case's own fictional in-scenario survey data (not an externally-checkable real-world claim) and is preserved as-is, unsourced, as scenario texture/filtering material in Appendix D -- consistent with how case-write's placeholder discipline treats fictional narrative data. All externally-checkable factual claims (Arizona's current GDL ages, the IIHS fatality table, the insurance-cost figure, the AAA per-mile driving cost, the FHWA average annual mileage figure, New Jersey's permit age, and Germany's BF17 law) are freshly sourced in 2026, not inherited from the 2021-vintage source document, via WebSearch/WebFetch -- see sources[] and RESEARCH_LOG.md.

balance.argument_a: Over the two years HB 3320 would delay licensure (age 16 to 18), a family avoids the full $4,050/year cost of insuring a 16-year-old -- $8,100 total -- while the extra chauffeuring the parent takes on, at a disclosed 6,000 mi/year and AAA's fully-loaded 66.37 cents/mile, costs $7,964.40. The dollar math favors AYE, even though it's close. The real safety case for AYE is not Appendix B's per-100,000-population table (which actually rises with age and does not support this reading -- see the Trap) -- it is Appendix B's separately cited per-mile statistic (S8): drivers 16-17 crash nearly twice as often per mile as drivers 18-19, the closest real, age-matched evidence that the youngest, least-experienced drivers carry the highest per-mile risk, even though S8's bands (16-17 vs 18-19) are not an exact match for this case's 15.5-vs-18 comparison.
balance.argument_b: The per-100,000-population data (Appendix B's main table) undercuts a naive 'raising the age makes it safer' argument in the most literal sense: that rate does not fall from 16 to 18 or 19 -- it keeps rising, because more of each age cohort is driving, and driving more, as they get older. Whatever HB 3320 buys, a clean per-capita safety win from that table is not automatically it (see FACILITATOR.md's Twist and the Trap). The real per-mile stat (S8) does favor AYE's safety case, but only at 16-17-vs-18-19 granularity, not this case's actual 15.5-vs-18 comparison -- a real gap a Hero can legitimately press on. And in dollar terms, NAY isn't just competitive, it's barely behind: $8,100 in extra insurance cost against $7,964.40 in extra chauffeuring cost is a $135.60 gap on a nearly $8,000 base -- and that entire gap sits inside a single disclosed, unsourced modeling assumption (MA1's 6,000 mi/year) that a Hero is fully entitled to challenge.
balance.margin_basis: Primary metric = net two-year dollar cost per family. Option A (raise to 18): MA1 miles (6,000/yr) x 2 years x AAA per-mile cost ($0.6637) = $7,964.40, insurance cost $0. Option B (keep 15.5): insurance increase $4,050/yr x 2 years = $8,100.00, chauffeuring cost $0. Margin = (8100.00 - 7964.40) / 7964.40 = 1.70%, Option A (AYE) cheaper.

derived._note: Computed during conversion from Appendix C's given data; case-readiness should re-derive independently via sensitivity_model.py.

modeling_assumptions.text: Extra annual miles a parent drives chauffeuring a non-driving 16-to-17-year-old is modeled at 6,000 miles/year -- roughly half the U.S. average annual per-car mileage (11,026 mi/year, Appendix C, S5), reflecting a teen's typical share of a family's driving (school, activities, work) rather than an adult's full driving load. No public dataset isolates parent-chauffeuring mileage specifically, so this is a disclosed, unsourced modeling choice, not a cited figure.

sensitivity_note: The 1.70% margin is real but extremely thin and sits entirely inside MA1's disclosed, unsourced chauffeuring-mileage assumption -- case-readiness Tier 2 probe 5 must be run and its finding disclosed here once available (see sensitivity_model.py FLEX list).

sensitivity_disclosure.justification: No public dataset isolates parent-chauffeuring mileage for a non-driving teen; the true quantity exists and varies by family but is not publicly measured anywhere. MA1's 6,000 mi/year is a documented good-faith estimate anchored to the closest public analogue (S5's FHWA average annual per-car mileage of 11,026 mi/year), not a citation for the actual figure. case-readiness Tier 2 probe 5 (2026-08-20) confirmed this dial is genuinely unstable: a -50% flex holds Option A's win but pushes the margin to 103.4% (breaks the SPEC section 2 20% cap), and a +50% flex both flips the winner to B and pushes the margin to 47.5% (also breaks the cap). This instability is disclosed here and in FACILITATOR.md's Sensitivity note rather than hidden -- the 1.70% base margin is real but rests entirely on this one estimated dial.

catalog.ask: Congresswoman Edmunds has to vote on raising Arizona's minimum driving age from 15½ to 18. Real crash-rate data can be read two ways depending on which trend line you draw -- and the two options cost Arizona families very different amounts of money.
